intro.title: There, at the DNA, is where epigenetics comes in.
intro.lead: Genes are relatively stable. Their activity is not. Epigenetics describes one part of the biological regulation through which cells respond to development, age, environment and lifestyle.

steps.title: The DNA stays.
steps.text: A person’s DNA sequence is relatively stable throughout much of life.

steps.title: The activity changes.
steps.text: Cells continuously regulate which genes are read more strongly or more weakly.

steps.title: The trend matters.
steps.text: Certain epigenetic patterns can change over the course of life.

chapters.question: What is epigenetics?
chapters.answer: Your genes stay largely the same. What changes is how active they are. Epigenetics describes how cells regulate the activity of genes without changing the DNA itself.
points: The DNA sequence is relatively stable throughout much of life.
Cells continuously regulate which genes are read more strongly or more weakly.
Certain epigenetic patterns can change over the course of life.
long: When it comes to genetics, many people think of an unchangeable blueprint. Indeed, a person’s DNA sequence is relatively stable throughout much of life. But genes are not equally active all the time: cells continuously regulate which genes are read more strongly or more weakly, when certain proteins are produced and how tissue adapts to strain.

This is exactly where epigenetics comes in. It studies mechanisms that influence the activity of genes without changing the DNA sequence. In this way, it helps to explain how predisposition and living environment interact.

This level is of particular interest for prevention, sports medicine, Healthy Aging and health advice: the basic genetic make-up remains largely constant, while certain epigenetic patterns can change over the course of life.

chapters.question: How is a gene turned up or down?
chapters.answer: Through three mechanisms that work together: marks on the DNA, the packaging of the DNA and small RNA molecules.
points: Methylation: small chemical groups sit at certain sites on the DNA.
Histones: the DNA is wrapped around proteins, sometimes more loosely, sometimes more tightly.
RNA: small RNA molecules can influence how a gene transcript is used.
long: Epigenetics is not a single switch. Several mechanisms interlock and influence how accessible genetic information is and how strongly it is used.

DNA methylation: small chemical groups are attached to certain sites on the DNA. Depending on the position, this can be associated with lower or higher gene activity. It is among the most frequently studied epigenetic mechanisms.

Histone modifications: in the cell nucleus, the DNA is wrapped around histone proteins. Chemical changes to these proteins can loosen or tighten the packaging and thereby influence how well certain regions can be read.

RNA regulation: microRNAs and other non-coding RNAs can influence how genetic information is processed and used after transcription. They are regarded as an important additional level of gene regulation.

chapters.question: What does my everyday life have to do with it?
chapters.answer: The body constantly responds to its surroundings. Some of these responses can be mediated or accompanied by epigenetic regulation.
points: This includes exercise, nutrition, sleep, stress, inflammation and ageing.
Pollutants, medication and social influences are also part of it.
Important: an epigenetic change is not automatically the cause of a disease.
long: The human organism continuously responds to its surroundings. This includes physical activity, nutrition, sleep, mental strain, inflammatory processes, pollutants, medication, social influences and ageing processes. Some of these responses can be mediated or accompanied by epigenetic regulation.
An epigenetic change is not automatically the cause of a disease. Studies often show associations at first. Whether a marker is a cause, a consequence or a bystander must be investigated separately.

chapters.question: What happens when stress meets the brain?
chapters.answer: Current models see mental health as an interplay of several levels: predisposition, environment, biological regulation, the brain and self-regulation.
points: This is being studied in anxiety disorders, depression, ADHD and chronic stress, among others.
Self-regulation means adapting feelings, attention, impulses and behaviour to demands.
Research on this is evolving; for now, many findings are associations.
long: Research is particularly exciting where environmental stressors meet the brain and behaviour. Modern models increasingly view mental health as a dynamic interplay of several levels: genetic predisposition, environment, biological regulation, brain function and psychological self-regulation.
Such relationships are being studied in anxiety disorders, depression, ADHD, post-traumatic stress disorder and states of chronic stress, among others.
A central concept is self-regulation: the ability to adapt emotions, attention, impulses, stress responses and behaviour to demands.

chapters.question: What does exercise do to the body?
chapters.answer: Training sends signals, and the body responds with adaptation. Regular exercise changes metabolism, blood vessels, muscle, the immune system and the brain.
points: Studies also describe epigenetic changes after training.
Previously trained muscle can rebuild certain adaptations more quickly after a break.
So far, part of this research comes from animal models. Caution is needed when applying this to individual people.
long: The environment does not act only as a stressor. Physical activity is a particularly clear example of how adaptable biological systems are. Regular exercise changes metabolism, vascular function, muscle, the immune system and the brain, and is increasingly also being linked to epigenetic changes.

After training, studies describe changes in DNA methylation, histone marks and regulatory RNAs, among others. These can be related to metabolic adaptations, mitochondrial function, regulation of inflammation and tissue repair.
Training generates mechanical, metabolic and hormonal signals. The body responds to them with adaptation.

In muscle, people often speak of “muscle memory”: previously trained muscle can rebuild certain adaptations more quickly after a break from training. Alongside neuromuscular and structural mechanisms, epigenetic explanations are also being studied.

Similar questions arise for metabolism, regulation of inflammation, the cardiovascular system and the brain. Above all, exercise early in life could leave longer-term biological effects. So far, part of this evidence comes from animal models, which is why statements about individual people must be worded cautiously.

chapters.question: What does an epigenetic age clock measure?
chapters.answer: It attempts to derive an ageing tendency from molecular data. It is not an exact measurement of “true biological age”.
points: Typical patterns of gene regulation change with age.
Results depend on the model, tissue, comparison group and measurement method.
Looking at the trend can be especially useful: how does a marker change over time?
long: With increasing age, characteristic patterns of gene regulation change. So-called epigenetic age clocks have been developed from DNA methylation patterns. They attempt to derive an ageing tendency from molecular data.

Such methods are scientifically interesting, but they are not identical to an exact measurement of “true biological age”. Results depend on the model, tissue, reference population and measurement method. Looking at the trend can therefore be especially useful: how does a marker change over time and in the context of documented lifestyle measures?

chapters.question: How do organs talk to each other during exercise?
chapters.answer: Through messenger molecules called exerkines. They can come from muscle, fat tissue, the liver and other organs.
points: They act on metabolism, blood vessels, the immune system and possibly the brain.
BDNF, FGF21, irisin and certain interleukins, among others, are being studied intensively.
This makes it understandable why exercise has effects far beyond the trained muscle.
long: Physical activity triggers the release of numerous signalling molecules. Such exercise-dependent messenger molecules are called exerkines. The intensively studied candidates include, among others, BDNF, FGF21, irisin and certain interleukins.
Epigenetic regulation can in turn influence how such signalling molecules are formed. This makes clear why exercise has effects far beyond the trained muscle.

chapters.question: What can epigenetic tests do – and what can they not?
chapters.answer: It is useful to look at the trend of selected markers in context. A diagnosis based on a single value is not useful.
points: Tests can be an additional basis for discussion in prevention and consultation.
A marker is not automatically a clear cause.
Measurement method, tissue, age, sex, medication and diseases always belong in the interpretation.
long: Useful: observing the trend of selected biomarkers; placing biological changes in the context of lifestyle and training; creating an additional basis for discussion in prevention and consultation.
Not useful: deriving a diagnosis from a single value; interpreting a marker as a clear cause; claiming that genes can be “reprogrammed” in a targeted way and at will.

Very important: taking into account the measurement method, tissue, age, sex, medication, diseases and temporal context. Results should always be placed within a larger clinical or preventive picture.

closing.quote: Our genes form the framework. Epigenetic regulation is one part of the body’s dynamic response to life, environment and behaviour.
closing.text: Between genetic predisposition and health outcome lies a complex regulatory system that responds to environment, development and behaviour. These responses are neither arbitrary nor fully controllable, but they are biologically real and increasingly measurable scientifically. Epigenetics should be neither overestimated nor underestimated: its greatest value at present lies in understanding biological adaptation in a more nuanced way and in better interpreting changes over time.
